sources.title: Human Rights and the Regulation of AI
sources.publisher: UK Parliament Joint Committee on Human Rights
sources.source_note: Primary parliamentary policy source. Recommendations are not enacted law. VALO links to the original publisher and does not republish the report.

evidence.proposition: The mere presence of a human in the loop is not sufficient to constitute meaningful human involvement or intervention; the person must be sufficiently informed and independent to reach an objective view not improperly influenced by the automated decision.
Human oversight can fail because people may be unable to scrutinise AI outputs effectively and may over-rely on automated outputs through automation bias.
evidence.evidence_type: committee finding based on witness evidence

evidence.proposition: AI systems posing a high risk of causing harm to human rights should require prior approval before they are provided or deployed.
Obligations should be distributed across the AI lifecycle and supply chain so risks are addressed by actors positioned to identify and prevent them.
Mandatory transparency should include disclosure that AI is being used, what it is being used for, and information about data sources when AI may significantly affect people or communities.

claims.text: Human presence in an AI workflow is not, by itself, evidence of effective human control.
For high-risk AI, deployment approval and the legitimacy of later operation are distinct questions.
Effective challenge and remedy require case-relevant information about AI use, not only a general description of a system.

analysis.text: Governance should distinguish representation of control from evidence of control. Policies, approval states and human-in-the-loop labels describe intended governance but do not by themselves prove that a concrete consequential action was legitimate and effectively controllable when it occurred.
